claim: Somatic hypermutation (SHM) is the diversity-generating process in antibody affinity maturation.
source: Somatic hypermutation (SHM) is the diversity-generating process in antibody affinity maturation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental support in this manuscript.

claim: Probabilistic models of SHM are needed for analyzing rare mutations, understanding the selective forces guiding affinity maturation, and understanding the underlying biochemical process.
source: Probabilistic models of SHM are needed for analyzing rare mutations, understanding the selective forces guiding affinity maturation, and understanding the underlying biochemical process.
evidence: This is a statement of motivation and rationale for the work, based on general understanding of the field.

claim: Recent work suggests the importance of a wider context for SHM.
source: We are motivated by recent work suggesting the importance of a wider context for SHM
evidence: This references prior work in the field, though specific citations are not provided in this sentence.

claim: Assigning an independent rate to each k-mer leads to an exponential proliferation of parameters.
source: however, assigning an independent rate to each k-mer leads to an exponential proliferation of parameters.
evidence: This is a mathematical fact about combinatorial growth of parameters.

claim: Thrifty models of SHM using convolutions on 3-mer embeddings can have fewer free parameters than a 5-mer model and yet have a significantly wider context.
source: Thus, using convolutions on 3-mer embeddings, we develop 'thrifty' models of SHM of various sizes; these can have fewer free parameters than a 5-mer model and yet have a significantly wider context.
evidence: This is supported by the model architecture described and parameter counts shown in Table 1.

claim: Thrifty models offer a slight performance improvement over a 5-mer model.
source: These offer a slight performance improvement over a 5-mer model
evidence: This is supported by performance metrics shown in Figure 2 and related figures.

claim: Other modern model elaborations worsen performance.
source: and other modern model elaborations worsen performance.
evidence: This is stated based on experimental results described in the Results section.

claim: A per-site effect is not necessary to explain SHM patterns given nucleotide context.
source: We also find that a per-site effect is not necessary to explain SHM patterns given nucleotide context.
evidence: This is supported by model comparison results showing that adding per-site rates did not improve out-of-sample performance.

claim: The two current methods for fitting an SHM model—on out-of-frame sequence data and on synonymous mutations—produce significantly different results.
source: Also, the two current methods for fitting an SHM model—on out-of-frame sequence data and on synonymous mutations—produce significantly different results
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 4 and related supplementary figures.

claim: Augmenting out-of-frame data with synonymous mutations does not aid out-of-sample performance.
source: and augmenting out-of-frame data with synonymous mutations does not aid out-of-sample performance.
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Antibodies are an essential component of the adaptive immune response.
source: Antibodies are an essential component of the adaptive immune response.
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge.

claim: Antibodies are secreted by B cells.
source: They are secreted by B cells
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge.

claim: When displayed on the surface of B cells, antibodies are called B cell receptors.
source: and when displayed on the surface of B cells are called B cell receptors.
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge.

claim: When stimulated by antigen binding, B cells undergo a process called 'affinity maturation' which involves mutation and selection.
source: When stimulated by antigen binding, B cells undergo a process called 'affinity maturation' which involves mutation and selection.
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge.

claim: The mutation process in affinity maturation happens at a very high rate relative to the rate of normal somatic mutation.
source: The mutation process happens at a very high rate relative to the rate of normal somatic mutation and is called somatic hypermutation (SHM).
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge.

claim: SHM is generated by a complex collection of interacting pathways of DNA damage and error-prone repair.
source: It is generated by a complex collection of interacting pathways of DNA damage and error-prone repair, which have been elucidated through decades of research (Wagner and Neuberger, 1996; Teng and Papavasiliou, 2007; Methot and Di Noia, 2017; Pilzecker and Jacobs, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: SHM pathways lead to a very non-uniform distribution of mutations.
source: These pathways lead to a very non-uniform distribution of mutations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SHM supported by the cited literature.

claim: The mutation biases in SHM are predictable from local sequence context.
source: Furthermore, the mutation biases are predictable from local sequence context.
evidence: This is supported by the extensive literature on SHM modeling cited in the following sentences.

claim: Many papers have investigated predictors of mutation rates from molecular sequence, including early work establishing the biases and parametric models estimating the mutability based on local sequence 'motif'.
source: Many papers have investigated predictors of mutation rates from molecular sequence, including early work establishing the biases (Dunn-Walters et al., 1998; Rogozin and Kolchanov, 1992; Rogozin and Diaz, 2004), to parametric models estimating the mutability based on local sequence 'motif', or sequence neighborhood around a focal base (Yaari et al., 2013; Elhanati et al., 2015; Cui et al., 2016; Feng et al., 2019; Fisher et al., 2025).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: SHM models are important when predicting the probability of amino acid changes in affinity maturation.
source: Such models are important when predicting the probability of amino acid changes in affinity maturation, for example, for understanding the prospects of selecting such mutations in reverse vaccinology (Martin Beem et al., 2023; Wiehe et al., 2018) or in computing a model of natural selection on antibodies (McCoy et al., 2015; Hoehn et al., 2017; Hoehn et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to applications of SHM models.

claim: The S5F 5-mer model and its variants are the most popular models for SHM.
source: The most popular models for SHM are the S5F 5-mer model and its variants (Yaari et al., 2013; Cui et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original work and reflects field knowledge.

claim: The S5F 5-mer model has shown its worth for over a decade, including tasks such as predicting the probability of mutations to mature broadly neutralizing antibodies against HIV.
source: They have shown their worth for over a decade now, including tasks such as predicting the probability of mutations to mature broadly neutralizing antibodies against HIV (Wiehe et al., 2018; Wiehe et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to applications of the S5F model.

claim: Biological considerations suggest that a wider context should be considered for SHM modeling.
source: However, biological considerations suggest that a wider context should be considered.
evidence: This is inferred from biological understanding of SHM mechanisms described in subsequent sentences.

claim: The consensus view of SHM requires processes such as patch removal around a lesion created by the activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) enzyme and subsequent error-prone repair.
source: Indeed, the consensus view of SHM requires processes such as patch removal around a lesion created by the activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) enzyme (Pilzecker and Jacobs, 2019) and subsequent error-prone repair.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review of SHM mechanisms.

claim: The presence of an AID hotspot several bases away may influence the probability of a mutation at a focal base.
source: Thus, for example, the presence of an AID hotspot several bases away may influence the probability of a mutation at a focal base.
evidence: This is inferred from the biological mechanism of SHM involving patch removal.

claim: Mesoscale-level sequence effects on AID deamination potentially deriving from local DNA sequence flexibility have been discovered.
source: More recently, mesoscale-level sequence effects on AID deamination potentially deriving from local DNA sequence flexibility have been discovered (Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: Position in the sequence can influence SHM.
source: In addition, other work has found that position in the sequence can influence SHM (Cohen et al., 2011; Spisak et al., 2020; Zhou and Kleinstein, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 7-mer models have been used for SHM prediction.
source: 7-mer models, which have three flanking bases on either side of the focal base, have been used (Elhanati et al., 2015; Marcou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: One cannot simply increase the size of the k-mer model indefinitely because the number of parameters grows exponentially with the size of the k-mer.
source: However, one cannot simply increase the size of the k-mer model indefinitely because the number of parameters grows exponentially with the size of the k-mer.
evidence: This is a mathematical fact about combinatorial parameter growth.

claim: More recent models of SHM include position-specific terms.
source: More recent models of SHM include position-specific terms (Spisak et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Context models of size up to 21 parameterized by a convolutional neural network have been developed for SHM.
source: and context models of size up to 21 parameterized by a convolutional neural network (Tang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Models based on the transformer architecture have shown great success in other contexts.
source: In other contexts, models based on the transformer architecture, Vaswani et al., 2017 have shown great success
evidence: This is supported by citation and general knowledge of machine learning.

claim: Elaborations such as a per-site rate and transformer only harm out-of-sample performance.
source: On the other hand, we find that elaborations such as a per-site rate and transformer only harm out-of-sample performance.
evidence: This is supported by experimental results described in the Results section.

claim: There is a clear difference between training models to predict well on out-of-frame data, compared to training models to predict well on synonymous mutations.
source: We also find a clear difference between training models to predict well on out-of-frame data, compared to training models to predict well on synonymous mutations.
evidence: This is supported by results shown in Figure 4 and related figures.

claim: The authors have released an open-source Python package with pretrained models and a simple API.
source: To make these models useful for the community, we have released an open-source Python package https://github.com/matsengrp/netam (Matsen and Dumm, 2025), with pretrained models and a simple API.
evidence: This is a statement about software release.

claim: The analysis for this article is reproducible via a GitHub repository.
source: Our analysis for this article is reproducible via https://github.com/matsengrp/thrifty-experiments-1 (copy archived at Sung, 2025).
evidence: This is a statement about code availability.

claim: The objective is to predict the probability of observed SHM in a child sequence relative to a parent sequence.
source: Our objective in this project is to predict the probability of observed SHM in a child sequence relative to a parent sequence.
evidence: This is a statement of the research objective.

claim: The study follows previous work in overall goal and data setup.
source: We follow previous work (Spisak et al., 2020) in overall goal and data setup.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The study predicts mutations in BCR sequences that are out-of-frame.
source: Specifically, we predict mutations in BCR sequences that are out-of-frame, that is, such that the sequence cannot code for a productive receptor.
evidence: This is a description of the data and methods used.

claim: Out-of-frame sequences are less likely to have undergone selective pressure in the germinal centers and instead provide more information about the SHM process.
source: Because the data is out-of-frame, this means that the sequences under consideration are less likely to have undergone selective pressure in the germinal centers and instead provide more information about the SHM process.
evidence: This is an inference about the biological properties of out-of-frame sequences.

claim: The study provides more relevant parent sequences and predicts finer-scale events by using phylogenetic reconstruction and ancestral sequence inference on sequences clustered into clonal families.
source: We also provide more relevant parent sequences and predict finer-scale events by using phylogenetic reconstruction and ancestral sequence inference on sequences clustered into clonal families (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a description of the methods used, illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: The tree with ancestral sequences is split into pairs of parent and child sequences, called parent–child pairs.
source: We split the tree with ancestral sequences into pairs of parent and child sequences, which we call parent–child pairs.
evidence: This is a description of the data processing method.

claim: The study experiments with using synonymous mutation data by masking mutations from the loss function that are not synonymous.
source: We also experiment with using synonymous mutation data by masking mutations from the loss function that are not synonymous (below; details in 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a description of an experimental approach.

claim: In all models, the distribution of mutations at a particular site is assumed to be independent of mutations at all other sites (but not independent of context).
source: In all models, the distribution of mutations at a particular site is assumed to be independent of mutations at all other sites (but not independent of context).
evidence: This is a statement about model assumptions.

claim: The study follows many authors in estimating a per-site rate and a per-site probability distribution among the non-identical bases describing the base selected in the event of a mutation.
source: We follow many authors starting from Yaari et al., 2013 in estimating a per-site rate, as well as a per-site probability distribution among the non-identical bases describing the base selected in the event of a mutation.

claim: Similar assumptions have been made previously in SHM modeling.
source: Similar assumptions have been made previously (Levinstein Hallak and Rosset, 2022; Levinstein Hallak et al., 2018; Rosset, 2007; Spisak et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

source: We used two data sets, which we will call the briney and tang data sets.

source: The briney data (Briney et al., 2019) consists of samples from nine individuals, but two of these samples resulted in many more sequences than the rest.

claim: The Spisak et al., 2020 team did important work in processing the briney data.
source: We acknowledge the important work the Spisak et al., 2020 team did in processing the briney data.

claim: The tang data will be a further test set.
source: The tang data (Vergani et al., 2017; Tang et al., 2020) will be a further test set.

claim: Each 3-mer is mapped into an embedding space of a fixed dimension, and these embedding locations are trainable parameters of the model.
source: Each 3-mer is mapped into an embedding space of a fixed dimension, and these embedding locations are trainable parameters of the model.
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture.

claim: The embedding abstracts some SHM-relevant characteristics of that 3-mer.
source: The idea is that the embedding abstracts some SHM-relevant characteristics of that 3-mer.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what the embedding represents.

claim: Each sequence is represented as a matrix with (sequence length) rows and (embedding dimension) columns.
source: Each sequence is then represented as a matrix with (sequence length) rows and (embedding dimension) columns.
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture.

claim: Convolutional filters are applied to these matrices, with taller convolutional filters effectively increasing the context of the model.
source: We then apply convolutional filters to these matrices, with taller convolutional filters effectively increasing the context of the model.
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture.

claim: A kernel size of 11 gives effectively a 13-mer model (because of the additional base on either side of the 3-mer).
source: For example, a kernel size of 11 gives effectively a 13-mer model (because of the additional base on either side of the 3-mer).
evidence: This is an explanation of how kernel size relates to effective k-mer size.

claim: A simple linear layer is applied to the result of the convolutional step in order to get a mutation rate estimate for each site.
source: We then apply a simple linear layer to the result of this step in order to get a mutation rate estimate for each site.
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture.

claim: The two model outputs (per-site rate and CSP) can be made in three ways: joined, hybrid, or independent.
source: We make these two model outputs in three ways (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1): they can share everything except for the final layer ('joined' model), or they can share the embedding layer ('hybrid' model), or they can be estimated separately ('independent' model).
evidence: This is a description of model variants illustrated in figures.

claim: When the size of the kernel is increased, the number of parameters increases linearly, not exponentially.
source: A key difference with a full k-mer model is that when we increase the size of the kernel, the number of parameters increases linearly, not exponentially.

claim: The thriftiest well-performing model is effectively a 13-mer model with fewer parameters than a 5-mer model.
source: In this way, the thriftiest well-performing model is effectively a 13-mer model with fewer parameters than a 5-mer model
evidence: This is supported by the parameter counts in Table 1 and performance results.

claim: These models can be scaled among a variety of dimensions.
source: however, one can scale these models among a variety of dimensions (Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the different model configurations shown in Table 1.

claim: The models were implemented in PyTorch.
source: We implemented our models in PyTorch (Paszke, 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about implementation with citation.

claim: Because of the small size of these models, they are fast to train and use.
source: Because of the small size of these models, they are fast to train and use.
evidence: This is an inference from the model size.

claim: The hyperparameters for the models were selected with a run of Optuna early in the project and then fixed.
source: The hyperparameters for the models (Table 1) were selected with a run of Optuna (Akiba et al., 2019) early in the project and then fixed.
evidence: This is a description of the hyperparameter selection process with citation.

claim: Further optimization was not pursued because of the limited performance differences between the existing models.
source: Further optimization was not pursued because of the limited performance differences between the existing models.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental approach based on observed results.

claim: AUROC can be interpreted as the probability that the model correctly identifies sites that mutate as having higher mutability than those that do not.
source: AUROC can be interpreted as the probability that the model correctly identifies sites that mutate as having higher mutability than those that do not.
evidence: This is a standard interpretation of AUROC.

claim: If one randomly selects a positive–negative pair, the AUROC is the probability that the positive example is assigned a higher probability than the negative example.
source: In fact, if one randomly selects a positive–negative pair, the AUROC is the probability that the positive example is assigned a higher probability than the negative example.
evidence: This is a standard interpretation of AUROC.

claim: AUROC is sensitive to class imbalance.
source: However, this measure is sensitive to class imbalance, and we are in the imbalanced setting here because mutations are relatively rare.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AUROC and an observation about the data.

claim: AUPRC provides an alternative that is less sensitive to class imbalance effects.
source: AUPRC provides an alternative that is less sensitive to class imbalance effects (Ozenne et al., 2015; Saito and Rehmsmeier, 2015) because the precision is the fraction of positive predictions that are true positives.

claim: R-precision gives a sense of how accurate the model is among sites that are most mutable.
source: R-precision gives a sense of how accurate the model is among sites that are most mutable.

claim: Substitution accuracy is how frequently the predicted-most-likely base is the one to which a site mutates.
source: To evaluate performance at predicting per-base substitution probabilities (given a mutation occurred), we report substitution accuracy: how frequently is the predicted-most-likely base the one to which a site mutates?
evidence: This is a definition of the substitution accuracy metric.

claim: The thrifty CNN models gave a modest performance improvement for predictive metrics compared to existing models.
source: We found that the thrifty convolutional neural network (CNN) models gave a modest performance improvement for these predictive metrics compared to existing models (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the performance results shown in Figure 2 and supplements.

claim: The study compared to a 5-mer model trained in exactly the same way, as well as a reimplementation of the model of Spisak et al., 2020.
source: Specifically, we compared to a 5-mer model trained in exactly the same way, as well as a reimplementation of the model of Spisak et al., 2020.
evidence: This is a description of the comparison models.

claim: The reimplementation infers very similar parameters to the previous implementation.
source: We confirmed that our reimplementation infers very similar parameters to the previous implementation, although we add a slight regularization to avoid some aspects of the original model fit that appear to be artifacts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: Because the Spisak et al., 2020 model fits a per-site rate, and the briney data does not have full sequence coverage, all evaluation was limited to positions 80 to 319, inclusive.
source: Because the Spisak et al., 2020 model fits a per-site rate, and the briney data does not have full sequence coverage, we limited all evaluation to a region well covered by the briney data: positions 80 to 319, inclusive.
evidence: This is a description of the evaluation approach based on data properties.

claim: All metrics except substitution accuracy were better on data from a distinct sequencing experiment (tang data) than on held-out samples from the same sequencing experiment (briney data).
source: We were surprised to find that all metrics except substitution accuracy were better on data from a distinct sequencing experiment (tang data) than on held-out samples from the same sequencing experiment (briney data).
evidence: This is an observation from the performance results.

claim: The difference in performance between briney and tang data is attributed to a difference in sequencing error between the two experiments.
source: We attribute this to there being a difference in sequencing error between the two experiments.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the observed performance differences.

claim: The briney data allowed sequences with only a single UMI representative while the tang data required at least two sequences per UMI.
source: The briney data allowed sequences with only a single UMI representative (Spisak et al., 2020) while the tang data required at least two sequences per UMI (Tang et al., 2020).

claim: If the model is successfully learning substitution probabilities due to SHM rather than sequencing error, it would underestimate the number of substitutions at positions with a low probability of substitution in the briney data but not in the tang data.
source: If our model is successfully learning substitution probabilities due to SHM rather than the sequencing error, we would expect our model to underestimate the number of substitutions at positions with a low probability of substitution in the briney data (which we expect to have more sequencing error) but not in the tang data (which we expect to have less sequencing error).
evidence: This is a prediction based on inference about model behavior.

claim: The predicted pattern of underestimation is what is observed in the characterization of model fit.
source: This is in fact what we see in our characterization of model fit below.
evidence: This refers to results shown in subsequent figures.

claim: The per-site rate did not seem to help the 5-mer model on held-out data, despite the results of Spisak et al., 2020.
source: We were also surprised to find that the per-site rate did not seem to help the 5-mer model on held-out data, despite the results of Spisak et al., 2020; see 'Discussion'.
evidence: This is an observation from the performance results that contrasts with previous work.

claim: There was not a substantial performance improvement by increasing the number of parameters of the CNNs.
source: We did not see a substantial performance improvement by increasing the number of parameters of the CNNs.
evidence: This is an observation from the performance results.

claim: The 'Large Indep' model that has the most flexibility may do a slightly better job with held-out samples from the same experiment in terms of substitution accuracy.
source: Although the 'Large Indep' model that has the most flexibility may do a slightly better job with held-out samples from the same experiment in terms of substitution accuracy, it does not appear any better when considering data from another experiment.

claim: The study compared work to a previous deep neural network model of SHM (Tang et al., 2022), which was trained on the tang data set.
source: We also compared our work to a previous deep neural network model of SHM (Tang et al., 2022), which was trained on the tang data set.
evidence: This is a description of a comparison with citation.

claim: A DeepSHM model consists of a pair of CNN models, one for estimating mutation frequencies and another for CSPs; this is akin to the 'independent' model configuration.
source: A DeepSHM model consists of a pair of CNN models, one for estimating mutation frequencies and another for CSPs; this is akin to our 'independent' model configuration.

source: Each of these CNNs has over 250,000 parameters, so in total is about 100 times larger than the largest CNN model we trained.

claim: The thrifty models performed comparably to DeepSHM when trained on the tang data only.

claim: When training in the usual way using the briney data and evaluating on synonymous data, the models do significantly worse than the S5F model, which was trained on synonymous mutations.
source: Furthermore, when we train in the usual way using the briney data and evaluate on synonymous data, we do significantly worse than the S5F model, which was trained on synonymous mutations (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by results shown in Figure 4 and supplements.

claim: The two sources of data (out-of-frame and synonymous) capture the effect of different processes.
source: Our conclusion is that these two sources of data capture the effect of different processes.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental results.

claim: By using an overlapping 3-mer embedding approach, wide-context models can be parameterized with relatively few parameters.
source: Specifically, by using an overlapping 3-mer embedding approach, we can parameterize wide-context models with relatively few parameters.
evidence: This is a summary of the modeling approach and its properties.

claim: A 13-mer model can be parameterized with fewer parameters than a 5-mer model with better out-of-sample performance.
source: For example, we can parameterize a 13-mer model with fewer parameters than a 5-mer model with better out-of-sample performance.
evidence: This is supported by the parameter counts in Table 1 and performance results.

claim: A similar approach of embedded k-mers has been successful previously for genome regulatory element function prediction.
source: A similar approach of embedded k-mers has been successful previously for genome regulatory element function prediction (Ji et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The thrifty models are better than previous models using a 5-mer context, but only slightly so.
source: Our first main result is that these models are better than previous models using a 5-mer context, but only slightly so.
evidence: This is a summary of the performance results.

claim: The modest improvement is interesting given that more distant effects are well motivated biologically.
source: This is interesting given that more distant effects are well motivated biologically, both in terms of the consensus model of SHM involving DNA damage, stripping, and repair (Pilzecker and Jacobs, 2019), as well as more recent results showing that the mesoscale environment of the BCR is important for SHM (Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in light of biological knowledge with citations.

claim: The present approach should be able to pick up features such as a nearby AID hotspot.
source: Although another model formulation may be able to pick up these features, the present approach should be able to pick up features such as a nearby AID hotspot.
evidence: This is an inference about model capabilities.

claim: Adding a per-site rate to the models did not help predict on out-of-sample data.
source: We found that adding a per-site rate to our models did not help predict on out-of-sample data.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental results.

claim: This finding contrasts with recent work of Spisak et al., 2020 suggesting that a per-site rate was helpful to predict SHM.
source: This is in contrast to recent work of Spisak et al., 2020 suggesting that a per-site rate was helpful to predict SHM.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work with citation.

claim: The contrast may be because of the means of evaluating the Spisak et al., 2020 model.
source: We suspect that this contrast may be because of the means of evaluating this model.
evidence: This is speculation about the reason for different results.

claim: The Spisak et al., 2020 model is itself parameterized in a per-site way, so it is not surprising that the model has excellent fit according to the Pearson r² metric.
source: The Spisak et al., 2020 model is itself parameterized in a per-site way, and so it is not surprising that the model has excellent fit according to this metric (Figure 4J of Spisak et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference about why the previous model performed well on that metric.

claim: The Spisak et al., 2020 data split was on the level of parent–child pairs.
source: Although they did a data-splitting exercise, this data split was on the level of parent–child pairs (not specified in the original paper; clarified via personal communication)
evidence: This is information obtained through personal communication.

claim: Many of the parent sequences in the Spisak et al., 2020 training set were very similar to parent sequences in the test set.
source: which means that many of the parent sequences in the training set were very similar to parent sequences (Spisak et al., 2020)
evidence: This is an inference about data leakage in the previous work.

claim: Other means of adding per-site rates to the model, such as positional encoding and a transformer component, did not help.
source: We tried other means of adding per-site rates to the model, such as positional encoding and a transformer component, but these did not help.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental results.

claim: It is quite possible that sites evolve differently according to their absolute position in the sequence.
source: Although it is quite possible that sites evolve differently according to their absolute position in the sequence, our work shows that this is not necessary as part of a predictive model.
evidence: This acknowledges a possibility while stating the empirical finding.

claim: It is difficult or perhaps impossible to disentangle the effect of a per-site rate from the effect of the motif model given a sufficiently rich motif model.
source: Due to commonalities between neighborhoods of sites in sequences, it is difficult or perhaps impossible to disentangle the effect of a per-site rate from the effect of the motif model given a sufficiently rich motif model.
evidence: This is an inference about model identifiability.

claim: While per-site rate and mesoscale-level effects may exist in SHM, their impact appears insufficient to significantly enhance statistical modeling performance.
source: From a biological perspective, our findings indicate that while per-site rate (Cohen et al., 2011; Spisak et al., 2020; Zhou and Kleinstein, 2020) and mesoscale-level (Wang et al., 2023) effects may exist in SHM, their impact appears insufficient to significantly enhance statistical modeling performance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results with citations.

claim: More definitive biological conclusions require an explicitly mechanistic model.
source: We refrain from making further biological conclusions and suggest that more definitive conclusions require an explicitly mechanistic model (Fisher et al., 2025).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current approach with citation.

claim: The two main ways of training a neutral model are to use synonymous mutations or to use out-of-frame sequences.
source: Our work also contrasts the two main ways of training a neutral model: one is to use synonymous mutations (Yaari et al., 2012), and the other is to use out-of-frame sequences (Spisak et al., 2020) or some other sequences that one can assume are evolving neutrally (Cui et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of two approaches with citations.

claim: These two methods give different results and models trained on one task do not do well on the other.
source: Here we find evidence that these two methods give different results and that models trained on one task do not do well on the other.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The difference between synonymous and out-of-frame results may be from synonymous mutations being under selection due to codon usage effects.
source: This may be from synonymous mutations being under selection due to codon usage effects
evidence: This is speculation about the cause of observed differences.

claim: The difference may be from only a subset of motifs being possible to estimate from synonymous data.
source: or could be from only a subset of motifs being possible to estimate from synonymous data (Yaari et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculation about the cause with citation.

claim: The spatial correlation of mutations could lead to correlation in mutations at synonymous and non-synonymous sites.
source: Another possible explanation is that the spatial correlation of mutations (Spisak et al., 2020) leads to correlation in mutations at synonymous and non-synonymous sites: as an extreme example, a fourfold synonymous site could be next to a site under strong purifying selection, and if these two sites only mutate together this would effectively lead to purifying selection on the synonymous site.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism with citation.

claim: One could imagine that the out-of-frame sequences are under selection such as having an insertion–deletion mutation that throws a sequence under selection out of frame.
source: One could also imagine that the out-of-frame sequences are under selection such as having an insertion–deletion mutation that throws a sequence under selection out of frame, but this is mitigated by the ancestral sequence reconstruction and the removal of the naive sequence from the tree.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible confound and how it is addressed.

claim: From a model-fitting perspective, the contrast between out-of-frame and synonymous objectives is disappointing because productive sequences are much more available than out-of-frame sequences.
source: From a model-fitting perspective, the contrast between these two objectives is disappointing because productive sequences are much more available than out-of-frame sequences.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the practical implications of the findings.

claim: A slight improvement was found using parameter sparse or 'thrifty' CNNs.
source: Overall, we have presented and tested a variety of new models with test–train splits and found a slight improvement using parameter sparse or 'thrifty' CNNs.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: One interesting aspect of these models is that they allow for a wider k-mer context without having a parameter explosion.
source: One interesting aspect of these models is that they allow for a wider k-mer context without having a parameter explosion.
evidence: This is a statement about a key property of the models.

claim: It is possible that the conclusions would differ if considerably more data were available.
source: It is possible that the conclusions would differ if we had considerably more data
evidence: This is speculation about how results might change with more data.

claim: Despite best efforts, the authors were unable to find a large additional volume of out-of-frame data.
source: though despite our best efforts (see 'Materials and methods') we were unable to find a large additional volume of out-of-frame data.
evidence: This is a statement about data availability efforts.

claim: If and when additional data becomes available, the reproducible analysis can be used to evaluate these models on that data.
source: If and when additional data becomes available, our reproducible analysis can be used to evaluate these models on that data.
evidence: This is a statement about future work possibilities.

claim: The primary data set consists of human, out-of-frame IgH sequences sampled from several individuals, aligned using pRESTO.
source: The data consists of human, out-of-frame IgH sequences sampled from several individuals (Briney et al., 2019), aligned using pRESTO (Vander Heiden et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the data with citations.

claim: The resulting data comes as a collection of trees, one for each clonal family with at least six observed sequences in an individual, complete with sequences and branch lengths, as well as metadata.
source: The resulting data comes to us as a collection of trees, one for each clonal family with at least six observed sequences in an individual, complete with (ancestral and observed) sequences and branch lengths, as well as a collection of metadata annotating, among other things, the identity and position of the V gene in the sequence.
evidence: This is a description of the data structure.

claim: Sequences containing gaps were removed to avoid ambiguity of site positions due to insertions or deletions.
source: Starting from the clonal family clustering and multiple sequence alignments from Spisak et al., 2020, we remove sequences containing gaps to avoid ambiguity of site positions due to insertions or deletions.
evidence: This is a description of data processing with rationale.

claim: Resulting clonal families with less than six observed sequences are discarded.
source: Resulting clonal families with less than six observed sequences are discarded.
evidence: This is a description of data filtering.

claim: Phylogenetic inference in each clonal family was redone with IQ-TREE.
source: Phylogenetic inference in each clonal family is then redone with IQ-TREE (Minh et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method with citation.

claim: The K80 substitution model was applied and the germline sequence was used as an outgroup, following the method of Spisak et al., 2020.
source: We apply the K80 (Kimura, 1980) substitution model and use the germline sequence as an outgroup, following the method of Spisak et al., 2020
evidence: This is a description of the phylogenetic method with citations.

claim: Mutation rate heterogeneity among sites was allowed with a four-category FreeRate model.
source: and additionally allow for mutation rate heterogeneity among sites with a four-category FreeRate model Soubrier et al., 2012; Yang, 1995.
evidence: This is a description of the phylogenetic model with citations.

claim: The edges of the inferred phylogenetic trees are taken as parent–child pairs, except for the edge containing the naive sequence outgroup.
source: The edges of the inferred phylogenetic trees are taken as parent–child pairs, except for the edge containing the naive sequence outgroup.
evidence: This is a description of how parent-child pairs are defined.

claim: The tang data set includes full-length BCR repertoires from 21 individuals.
source: This data set, originally generated by Tang et al., 2020; Vergani et al., 2017, includes full-length BCR repertoires from 21 individuals.
evidence: This is a description of the data with citations.

claim: Preprocessed samples were obtained directly from the authors.
source: We obtained preprocessed samples directly from the authors (Tang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about data acquisition with citation.

claim: IgH sequences were extracted from marginal zone (MZ), memory (M), and plasma (PC) B cells.
source: We extracted the IgH sequences from marginal zone (MZ), memory (M), and plasma (PC) B cells
evidence: This is a description of data processing.

claim: Germline and clonal family inferences were completed with partis.
source: and completed germline and clonal family inferences with partis (Ralph and Matsen, 2016a; Ralph and Matsen, 2016b; Ralph and Matsen, 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method with citations.

claim: Clonal families of two or more sequences that consist of only out-of-frame sequences were kept.
source: We keep clonal families of two or more sequences that consist of only out-of-frame sequences.
evidence: This is a description of data filtering.

claim: In partis, a sequence is considered out-of-frame if either of the conserved codons for cysteine or tryptophan bounding the CDR3 is out-of-frame with the germline V gene.
source: In partis, a sequence is considered out-of-frame if either of the conserved codons for cysteine or tryptophan bounding the CDR3 is out-of-frame with the germline V gene.
evidence: This is a description of how out-of-frame is defined in the software.

claim: Phylogenetic inference and ancestral sequence reconstruction were performed for each clonal family using IQ-TREE as described for the briney data.
source: We then perform phylogenetic inference and ancestral sequence reconstruction for each clonal family using IQ-TREE as described above.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method.

claim: The first site of the sequence is set to align with the start of the germline V gene.
source: The first site of the sequence is set to align with the start of the germline V gene
evidence: This is a description of sequence alignment.

claim: If necessary, nucleotides before the start of the V gene are truncated or sites at the 5' end with missing reads are padded with 'N'.
source: if necessary, nucleotides before the start of the V gene are truncated or sites at the 5' end with missing reads are padded with 'N'.
evidence: This is a description of sequence processing.

claim: A small number of the edges have very long branch lengths, some of which seem to correspond to improper alignments.
source: A small number of the edges have very long branch lengths, some of which seem to correspond to improper alignments.
evidence: This is an observation about data quality.

claim: Following Spisak et al., 2020, the data was filtered to only include edges with fewer than 10 mutations, which results in a modest ∼6.4% reduction in the available data.
source: Following the lead of the authors of Spisak et al., 2020, we filter our data to only include edges with fewer than 10 mutations, which results in a modest ∼6.4% reduction in the available data.
evidence: This is a description of data filtering with citation and quantification.

claim: The jaffe data set consists of paired heavy chain and light chain, full-length sequences of productive antibodies from four donors.
source: The jaffe data set (Jaffe et al., 2022) consists of paired heavy chain and light chain, full-length sequences of productive antibodies from four donors.
evidence: This is a description of the data with citation.

claim: The jaffe data was processed with partis and IQ-TREE, similar to the tang data set.
source: We process the data with partis and IQ-TREE, similar to the tang data set.
evidence: This is a description of data processing.

claim: The jaffe synonymous data set are parent–child pairs from jaffe where sites in the child sequence that are not fourfold degenerate in the parent context are masked.
source: The jaffe synonymous data set are parent–child pairs from jaffe where we mask sites in the child sequence that are not fourfold degenerate in the parent context.
evidence: This is a description of data processing.

claim: For each parent–child pair, each codon context in the parent sequence is checked for fourfold degenerate sites.
source: For each parent–child pair, we check each codon context in the parent sequence for fourfold degenerate sites.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method.

claim: For fourfold degenerate sites, the corresponding nucleotide in the child sequence is preserved while all other sites are masked.
source: For these sites, the corresponding nucleotide in the child sequence is preserved while all other sites are masked.
evidence: This is a description of data processing.

claim: The loss functions are the likelihood of child mutation locations using offset, as well as a categorical cross-entropy loss for the base identity.
source: Our loss functions are the likelihood of child mutation locations using offset, as well as a categorical cross-entropy loss for the base identity.
evidence: This is a description of the training objective.

claim: These log losses are summed together using a weight of 0.01 on the cross-entropy loss to approximately even out the contributions of these two sources of loss.
source: We sum these log losses together using a weight of 0.01 on the cross-entropy loss to approximately even out the contributions of these two sources of loss.
evidence: This is a description of the training procedure.

claim: Models were trained for 100 epochs, with the Poisson offset simply being the normalized count of mutations in the child sequence.
source: Models were trained for 100 epochs, with the Poisson offset simply being the normalized count of mutations in the child sequence.
evidence: This is a description of the training procedure.

claim: A more sophisticated approach of joint optimization of branch length and model parameters was also tried.
source: We also tried a more sophisticated approach of joint optimization of branch length and model parameters.
evidence: This is a description of an alternative training approach.

claim: Full-length IgH data is generally limited by design in common sequencing approaches.
source: Full-length IgH data is generally limited by design in common sequencing approaches.
evidence: This is a statement about data availability in the field.

claim: Even productive IgH data show low coverage at the start of the V gene, as evidenced by over 40% of the sequences in the Observed Antibody Space (OAS) database lacking sequence data for the first 15 amino acids.
source: Even productive IgH data show low coverage at the start of the V gene, as evidenced by over 40% of the sequences in the Observed Antibody Space (OAS) database lacking sequence data for the first 15 amino acids (Olsen et al., 2022b; Kovaltsuk et al., 2018; Olsen et al., 2022a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to database analyses.

claim: Out-of-frame sequences make up a relatively small proportion of sequence data, with this proportion varying by study/sequencing protocols.
source: Overall, out-of-frame sequences make up a relatively small proportion of sequence data (with this proportion varying by study/sequencing protocols)
evidence: This is an observation from the data search efforts.

claim: None of the additional data sets considered had enough depth to extract a meaningful amount of out-of-frame sequence data for the study's purposes.
source: and none of the data sets considered had enough depth to extract a meaningful amount of out-of-frame sequence data for our purposes.
evidence: This is a summary of the data search results.
